'''Barbara E. Ehrlich''' is Professor of Pharmacology and of Cellular and Molecular Physiology at [[Yale University]] working on the biophysics of membrane ion channels. Recent research investigates the function of [[polycystin-2]], the [[inositol trisphosphate receptor]], and the [[ryanodine receptor]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kuo|first1=IY|last2=Ehrlich|first2=BE|title=Muscling in on the ryanodine receptor.|journal=Nature Structural & Molecular Biology|date=February 2015|volume=22|issue=2|pages=106–7|pmid=25650905|doi=10.1038/nsmb.2960|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Yang|first1=Y|last2=Keeler|first2=C|last3=Kuo|first3=IY|last4=Lolis|first4=EJ|last5=Ehrlich|first5=BE|last6=Hodsdon|first6=ME|title=Oligomerization of the polycystin-2 C-terminal tail and effects on its Ca2+-binding properties.|journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry|date=17 April 2015|volume=290|issue=16|pages=10544–54|pmid=25716316|doi=10.1074/jbc.m115.641803|pmc=4400361|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bezprozvanny|first1=I.|last2=Watras|first2=J.|last3=Ehrlich|first3=B. E.|date=1991-06-27|title=Bell-shaped calcium-response curves of Ins(1,4,5)P3- and calcium-gated channels from endoplasmic reticulum of cerebellum|journal=Nature|volume=351|issue=6329|pages=751–754|doi=10.1038/351751a0|issn=0028-0836|pmid=1648178|bibcode=1991Natur.351..751B|s2cid=4340204}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Ehrlich was born in New London, CT in 1952 and grew up in Newport, RI. Ehrlich attended [[Brown University]], where she received a [[Bachelor of Science]]: ScB in Applied Mathematics and Biology.<ref name=":1"/> She then received her PhD from the [[University of California at Los Angeles]] in 1979 on the topic of membrane transport parameters in bipolar disorder.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ehrlich|first1=BE|last2=Diamond|first2=JM|last3=Gosenfeld|first3=JL|last4=Kaufman-Diamond|first4=S|title=Lithium, membranes, and manic-depressive illness|journal=Psychopharmacology Bulletin|date=1978|volume=14|issue=3|page=21}}</ref> In 1974 she was a pre-doctoral Student at Brown University and Mount Desert Island Biological Laboratory, Providence, RI and Salsbury Cove, ME. Her research focused on iodide transport in the choroid plexus epithelium.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Barbara Ehrlich, PhD |url=https://medicine.yale.edu/profile/barbara-ehrlich/ |access-date=2026-02-16 |website=medicine.yale.edu |language=en}}</ref>

== Career ==
At [[Brown University]], Ehrlich worked with [[Helen Cserr]], Professor of Physiology. Her doctoral advisor was [[Jared Diamond]] and she studied lithium transport in human red blood cells as a way to understand lithium treatment in bipolar disorder. Ehrlich completed her post doctoral research at the [[Albert Einstein College of Medicine]] and the [[Marine Biological Laboratory]] at Woods Hole.<ref name=":1"/> In 1972, while working at the Marine Biological Laboratory, Ehrlich experienced gender discrimination as a woman in science. She had to advocate for her opportunity to attend scientific lectures and became the only woman participating in them.[https://sites.brown.edu/pembrokeoralhistory/2023/07/06/barbara-e-ehrlich-class-of-1974/] She then went on to work as a professor at the [[University of Connecticut]] for 11 years. At the University of Connecticut, she coined the term "Molecular [[Hermeneutics]]." Hermeneutics is a philosophical discipline derived from [[Hermes]], who was the Messenger of the Gods and had to both deliver and interpret messages. Hermeneutics became the exegesis of the [[Bible]], and eventually it evolved to interpretation, in particular of Truth and Beauty.<ref>{{Citation|last=Mantzavinos|first=C.|title=Hermeneutics|date=2016|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2016/entries/hermeneutics/|encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|editor-last=Zalta|editor-first=Edward N.|edition=Winter 2016|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|access-date=2019-07-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jgp-soundsphys.rupress.org/2015/01/26/barbara-ehrlich/|title=Molecular hermeneutics and unusual sorbets: Barbara Ehrlich|last=Press|first=Rockefeller University|date=2015-01-26|website=Sounds Physiological|language=en|access-date=2019-07-19}}</ref> She continues to be the Director of the Laboratory of Molecular Hermeneutics at [[Yale University]], where she presently works.

Ehrlich began working at [[Yale University]] in 1997 as a professor of [[pharmacology]] and of cellular and molecular physiology.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://medicine.yale.edu/bbs/people/barbara_ehrlich.profile|title=Barbara Ehrlich, PhD > Biological & Biomedical Sciences {{!}} Yale University|website=medicine.yale.edu|access-date=2019-07-19}}</ref> At Yale, Ehrlich has mainly focused on intracellular calcium regulation.<ref name=":1"/> Her laboratory uses [[calcium imaging]] combined with [[electrophysiological]], [[biochemical]], and molecular techniques to study the classes of calcium release channels known to exist inside virtually all cells: the [[inositol trisphosphate receptor]]-gated channel, the [[ryanodine receptor]], and [[polycystin 2]]. Ehrlich and her team work to understand the loss of calcium regulation observed in disease states as seen in cells from patients with [[polycystic kidney disease]] or leading to drug-induced [[peripheral neuropathy]]. The Ehrlich team hypothesizes that these abnormalities in function are consequences, at least in part, of altered intracellular calcium homeostasis and that these studies will lead to suitable treatment regimens.<ref name=":1"/>

From 2004 to 2011, Ehrlich was on the board of scientific counselors at the [[Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development]].<ref name=":1" />

== Personal life ==
Ehrlich was married to Lawrence B. Cohen, Professor of Cellular and Molecular Physiology at [[Yale University]]. Ehrlich has one daughter, and is presently married to Stuart M. Johnson. Ehrlich splits her time between New York City and New Haven, Connecticut.{{Citation needed|date=October 2019}}
